seoDescription: Hurt at work in Ann Arbor, at the University, a hospital, a research lab, a construction site, a restaurant, or on the road? Michigan workers’ comp owes you 80 percent of your after-tax wage up to a weekly maximum, and all medical care. The benefits, the 90-day notice and two-year claim, the 28-day doctor rule, occupational disease, student and graduate employees, federal workers, and the third-party suit comp does not bar, including the six-month notice when the University is the third party. Free review. (313) 406-7606.
tagline: Ann Arbor’s work runs from University classrooms, labs, and hospitals to construction sites, restaurants, and delivery routes. Michigan’s Act gives an injured worker 80 percent of after-tax wages up to a weekly maximum, every medical bill, and a hearing. It also gives 90 days to report the injury.

sections.heading: Where Ann Arbor workers are hurt, and who handles the claim

c.v: The University and Michigan Medicine employ tens of thousands of people in Ann Arbor, and the injuries span every kind of work:

items.v: patient-handling injuries to backs and shoulders from lifting and transfers
needlesticks, exposures, and assaults by patients in the hospitals
slips on wet floors, ice on campus walks, and falls in parking structures
custodial, grounds, food-service, and maintenance injuries
repetitive-strain injuries in offices and labs

c.v: A University employee’s comp claim is against the University as the employer, under the same Act, before the same agency. The University’s Work Connections office administers its employees’ claims. Because the University is the State, comp remains the exclusive remedy against it, and any separate claim against the University itself, as described below, follows the State’s rules.

Many University workers are students: student employees in dining halls, libraries, and labs, and graduate students who teach or do research. A student who is paid as an employee is generally covered. Whether a graduate student is an employee for comp purposes can depend on how the position is classified and paid, for example as a teaching or staff assistant or on a fellowship. A student hurt in a class or an unpaid internship is usually not an employee, and the claim, if any, is an ordinary injury claim.
Lab work produces injuries offices do not:

items.v: chemical burns and exposures
needlesticks and biological exposures
animal bites and allergies in animal research
cuts and crush injuries in machine shops and prototype labs

For that kind of claim, the date of injury is generally the last day of work in the employment that caused it, and the 90-day notice runs from when the worker knew, or should have known, that the condition was work-related (MCL 418.301(1), 418.381(1)). Write down what you were exposed to, when, and in what lab.
Other hospitals, nursing homes, and home care.

Nurses, aides, and technicians at Trinity Health Ann Arbor, clinics, nursing homes, and assisted living communities have the same patient-handling and exposure injuries. Health care workers’ injuries are often cumulative, and the insurer may argue the condition is degenerative rather than work-related (see “wear and tear” below). Home-care aides injured in a client’s home have a comp claim against their agency and, where a hazard in the home caused the injury, possibly a premises claim against the homeowner.
Campus, hospital, and downtown projects, and road work on the corridors and freeways, produce:

items.v: falls from ladders, scaffolds, roofs, and openings
struck-by and caught-between injuries, including by cranes, concrete trucks, and dump trucks
trench collapses
electrocutions
work-zone injuries from passing traffic

c.v: Most construction workers are employed by a subcontractor. Their comp claim is against their own employer. A general contractor, another subcontractor, a property owner, or an equipment maker may be sued as a third party (see below). On a University project, a claim against the University is a claim against the State. It must fit an immunity exception, such as a dangerous condition of a public building (with notice within 120 days, MCL 691.1406) or a University vehicle (with notice within six months, MCL 600.6431), and both notices are filed with the Court of Claims. Some small employers carry no workers’ compensation insurance.

items.v: An uninsured employer loses the exclusive-remedy protection. The worker may claim comp benefits and may also sue the employer in circuit court, and officers can be personally liable (MCL 418.641, 418.647).

c.v: Office work produces fewer traumatic injuries but real ones: falls on icy walks and parking-structure ramps, and repetitive-strain injuries to wrists, elbows, and necks. Two rules matter:

items.v: An injury on the way to or from work is generally not covered, but an injury in the employer’s parking lot or structure, or while traveling for work, generally is (MCL 418.301(3)).
An injury while working from home can be covered if it arose out of and in the course of the work. The facts of exactly what you were doing decide it.

c.v: Many employers offer employer-paid short- and long-term disability that is coordinated with comp (MCL 418.354).

Comp pays 80 percent of after-tax wages only up to the state maximum, about $1,201 a week for 2026 injuries. For a physician, engineer, researcher, or manager whose after-tax pay is well above that, the benefit replaces only part of the income. Comp is still the only remedy against the employer. But if someone other than the employer caused the injury, a third-party suit recovers the full wage loss, along with pain and suffering, which comp never pays.

The City of Ann Arbor, including police and fire; Ann Arbor Public Schools; Washtenaw Community College; Washtenaw County; and TheRide. The injuries are public-safety injuries, custodial and maintenance injuries, bus operators’ injuries, and assaults. Public employers have pension and duty-disability provisions that run alongside comp. Police officers and firefighters have a statutory presumption for certain heart and respiratory conditions (MCL 418.405).

Workers at the VA Ann Arbor Healthcare System, the post office, and other federal offices in the city are not covered by Michigan’s Act. Their claims fall under the Federal Employees’ Compensation Act, administered by the U.S. Department of Labor:

items.v: a different benefit rate (two-thirds of pay, or three-quarters with a dependent)
continuation of regular pay for up to 45 days after a traumatic injury, if the injury is reported promptly on the federal form
a three-year deadline for the claim, with shorter deadlines for continuation of pay
no Michigan magistrate hearing

c.v: Pre-existing conditions and wear and tear.

items.v: Years on a nursing unit, in a kitchen, at a keyboard, or on a construction site produce degenerative necks, shoulders, backs, and knees. The question is whether work contributed to or aggravated the condition in a significant manner (MCL 418.301(2)). The pre- and post-injury records decide it.
Parking-lot, travel, and work-from-home injuries are denied on this ground. The facts of where you were and what you were doing for the employer decide it.
Student workers, graduate students, delivery drivers, and staffing-agency workers are denied on this ground. The facts of the work, the pay, and the control decide it.
Refusing a job within your restrictions without good reason can end benefits (MCL 418.301(9)). Whether an offered job is real and within your limits is a common dispute.

sections.heading: The hearing, and the lawsuit comp does not bar

c.v: When an employer or insurer denies a claim or stops paying, the worker files an Application for Mediation or Hearing (Form WC-104A) with the Workers’ Disability Compensation Agency. Disputed claims go to mediation and then to a magistrate, with appeal to the Michigan Compensation Appellate Commission.
A contested claim often takes a year or more. That is why many disputed claims resolve by
, a lump-sum settlement approved by the magistrate that closes the claim, including future medical care (MCL 418.835). Do not sign one without advice.

Workers’ compensation is your exclusive remedy against an insured employer (MCL 418.131), with one narrow exception: an employer that specifically intended an injury, meaning it had actual knowledge that an injury was certain to occur and willfully disregarded that knowledge (MCL 418.131(1)).
You can sue anyone else whose negligence caused the injury (MCL 418.827):

items.v: in a crash on the job, with workers’ compensation primary and no-fault paying the difference (MCL 500.3109(1))

faqs.question: How long do I have to report a work injury in Ann Arbor?

answer.v: Ninety days from the injury, or from when you knew it was work-related, to notify your employer, and two years to file a claim. Report it in writing the day it happens.

faqs.question: I work for the University of Michigan. Is my claim different?

answer.v: The rules are the same Act and the same agency. The difference is that the University’s Work Connections office administers the claim, and comp is your only remedy against it. If someone other than the University caused the injury, you can also sue that person or company.

faqs.question: I’m a graduate student who teaches or does research. Am I covered?

answer.v: Often, if you are paid as an employee. Whether a graduate student is an employee for comp purposes can depend on how the position is classified and paid. Keep your appointment letter and pay records.

faqs.question: I was exposed to something in a lab and got sick months later. Is that comp?

answer.v: It can be. An illness caused by work exposure is an occupational disease. The 90-day notice generally runs from when you knew or should have known the illness was work-related. Write down the exposure and report it in writing.

faqs.question: I work for a contractor on a University project and was hurt by the University’s negligence. Can I sue the University?

answer.v: Possibly, as a third party. The claim is against the State and must fit an immunity exception, such as a defective public building or a University vehicle. Notice must be filed with the Court of Claims, within 120 days for a building or six months for a vehicle, in addition to your comp claim against your own employer.

faqs.question: I work at the VA. Is that Michigan workers’ comp?

answer.v: No. Federal employees are covered by the Federal Employees’ Compensation Act, with a different benefit rate, its own forms, and a three-year claim deadline. Report the injury on the federal form right away.

faqs.question: I slipped in my employer’s parking structure on the way in. Is that covered?

answer.v: Generally yes. The going-and-coming rule excludes the commute itself, but an injury in the employer’s parking lot or structure is usually treated as in the course of employment. If the building owner or a snow-removal contractor that is not your employer let the ice build up, you may also have a third-party claim.

faqs.question: My salary is well above the comp maximum. Is that all I get?

answer.v: From comp, the benefit is 80 percent of after-tax wages up to the weekly maximum. An employer disability plan may add to it, coordinated with comp. If someone other than your employer caused the injury, a third-party suit can recover the full wage loss and pain and suffering.

faqs.question: What does an Ann Arbor workers’ comp lawyer cost?

answer.v: Nothing up front. Fees are limited by state rule to a percentage of the benefits recovered and must be approved by the magistrate. You owe nothing if no benefits are recovered.
